title: Pseudo-classes & Pseudo-elements
summary: **Pseudo-classes** (`:hover`, `:focus`, `:nth-child`) style elements based on state or position, while **pseudo-elements** (`::before`, `::after`, `::placeholder`) style or create sub-parts of an element that don't exist in the DOM — together they power interactivity and decorative UI without extra markup.

subtopics.title: State pseudo-classes: :hover, :focus, :active
subtopics.explanation: These react to user interaction. :hover applies when the pointer is over an element, :focus when it receives keyboard/tab focus (critical for accessibility), and :active during the press. Always pair :hover with :focus so keyboard users get the same feedback, and consider :focus-visible to show outlines only for keyboard navigation.

subtopics.title: Structural pseudo-classes: :nth-child, :first-child, :last-child
subtopics.explanation: These match elements by their position among siblings. :first-child / :last-child target the ends; :nth-child(n) takes a formula like 2n (even), odd, or 3n+1. They count ALL siblings, so :nth-child(2) means 'this element AND it is the 2nd child'. Use :nth-of-type when you only want to count elements of the same tag.

subtopics.title: The negation pseudo-class :not()
subtopics.explanation: :not(selector) matches every element that does NOT match the inner selector — great for 'all but the last' spacing or excluding a variant. It takes the specificity of its most specific argument (the :not() itself adds none). Modern :not() accepts a comma list: :not(.a, .b).

subtopics.title: Form state: :checked, :disabled, :required
subtopics.explanation: Form pseudo-classes reflect input state. :checked targets checked checkboxes/radios and is the key to checkbox-only toggles (the 'CSS checkbox hack'). :disabled, :required, :valid, and :invalid let you style forms purely from their state without JavaScript.

subtopics.title: ::before and ::after with the content property
subtopics.explanation: ::before and ::after insert a generated inline box as the first/last child of an element. They REQUIRE a content property to render (even content: ""). Use them for icons, decorative shapes, tooltips, counters, and clearing floats — all without adding HTML. Generated content is not in the accessibility tree reliably, so don't put essential text there.

subtopics.title: ::placeholder, ::selection, ::first-line
subtopics.explanation: These style real sub-parts of an element. ::placeholder styles an input's placeholder text, ::selection changes the highlight color when a user selects text, and ::first-line / ::first-letter style typographic fragments. They are styling-only — you cannot bind events to them.

subtopics.title: Single colon vs double colon
subtopics.explanation: Pseudo-classes use a single colon (:hover); pseudo-elements use double colons (::before) since CSS3, to visually distinguish the two. For backward compatibility, the original four pseudo-elements (:before, :after, :first-line, :first-letter) still accept a single colon, but you should always write new pseudo-elements with ::.
subtopics.example:
.x::before { content: ""; } /* preferred */
.x:before  { content: ""; } /* legacy, still works */

subtopics.title: Combining for UI patterns
subtopics.explanation: Real components chain these: a custom checkbox uses input:checked + .ui, tooltips use [data-tip]:hover::after, zebra tables use :nth-child(even), and accordions use the :checked hack. Mastering the combinations lets you build interactive UI with zero JavaScript.

foundations.overview: Selectors normally target elements that literally exist in the HTML. Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements extend selectors to reach things the document tree doesn't directly expose: transient states (hovered, focused, checked), positions among siblings (first, nth), and virtual sub-parts of an element (the part before its content, its placeholder text, the user's selection). They let you style interaction and decoration declaratively, without extra DOM nodes or JavaScript.
foundations.formalDefinition: A pseudo-class is a keyword added to a selector (prefixed with :) that styles an element when it is in a particular state or matches a structural condition. A pseudo-element (prefixed with ::) styles a specific, often generated, sub-part of an element as if it were a separate element.
foundations.whyItMatters: Hover effects, focus outlines, zebra striping, placeholder colors, decorative icons, and CSS-only toggles all depend on them. They keep markup clean and are heavily tested in interviews — especially :nth-child math, the single-vs-double-colon rule, and the content property.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of pseudo-classes as 'when is this element?' filters and pseudo-elements as 'invisible extra children/regions' you can style. ::before is a tiny box CSS injects at the start of the element; :hover is a temporary label the browser sticks on while the mouse is over it.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser re-evaluates dynamic pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus, :checked) on every relevant event and recomputes matching styles. Generated pseudo-elements are created during box generation: the browser builds an anonymous box for ::before/::after only when content is set, then lays it out and paints it inline with the element's content.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Button and link states, accessible focus rings, table zebra striping, required-field indicators with ::after content, tooltips, custom checkboxes/radios, dropdown carets, and placeholder styling are all built with these.
foundations.businessImpact: Clear interactive feedback (hover/focus states) and accessible focus indicators improve usability and conversion, while CSS-only patterns reduce JavaScript payload and maintenance cost.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Using pseudo-elements for decoration removes 'spacer' and 'icon' divs, shrinking the DOM and simplifying components. Understanding specificity of :not() and structural selectors prevents cascade surprises.
foundations.performanceImpact: These selectors are cheap, but very broad dynamic selectors (e.g. * :hover) can cause excess style recalculation. Generated content is paint-only and avoids extra DOM nodes, which is generally faster than adding elements.
commonUseCases: Hover/focus/active states on buttons and links
Decorative icons and required markers via ::before / ::after content

commonMisconceptions.myth: ::before adds content after the element's opening tag in the DOM.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It generates an anonymous box inside the element's render tree but does not appear in the DOM; it needs a content property and isn't reliably exposed to assistive tech.
It counts ALL siblings, so it matches only if the element is literally the 2nd child overall. Use :nth-of-type(2) to count by tag.

visualExplorer.title: How ::before generates a box
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how the browser matches a pseudo-class state and injects a generated pseudo-element box.

steps.title: Selector parsed
steps.description: The browser reads button:hover::before and splits it into the element (button), a state condition (:hover), and a pseudo-element (::before).

steps.title: State evaluated
steps.description: On pointer move, the browser checks if the pointer is over the button. If so, the :hover condition matches and the rule becomes active.

steps.title: content checked
steps.description: For ::before, the browser looks for a content property. With content set, it creates an anonymous generated box; without it, nothing renders.

steps.title: Box generated
steps.description: An inline box is inserted as the first child of the button, laid out before the real text content.

steps.title: Painted
steps.description: The generated box is painted with its own styles (color, content, margin), updating live as the :hover state toggles.

interactiveExamples.title: Hover and focus states
interactiveExamples.explanation: The button changes color on :hover and shows an outline on :focus-visible so keyboard users get feedback too.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A blue button that darkens on hover/press and shows a light outline when focused via keyboard.

interactiveExamples.title: Zebra table with ::before required marker
interactiveExamples.explanation: :nth-child(even) stripes alternate rows, and ::after adds a red asterisk to required labels without extra HTML.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A table with alternating row shading and red asterisks after required field labels.

codeLab.title: Build a CSS-only custom checkbox
codeLab.instructions: Use the :checked pseudo-class and the sibling selector to style the label when the box is ticked, and ::before to draw a checkmark. Hint: input:checked + label and label::before.

files.index.html:
<input type="checkbox" id="agree">
<label for="agree">I agree to the terms</label>

codeLab.expectedOutput: Clicking the label toggles a custom box that fills green and shows a checkmark when checked.

files.index.html:
<input type="checkbox" id="agree">
<label for="agree">I agree to the terms</label>

hints: Hide the native input with display: none and style the label instead.
input:checked + label::before lets you change the generated box only when the input is checked.
Set content to a checkmark escape (\2713) on the checked state.

debuggingLab.title: Why doesn't ::before show up?
debuggingLab.symptom: A ::before rule with color and margin is written, but nothing appears on the page.

files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 30px; font-size: 24px; }
.price::before { color: #16a34a; font-weight: 700; }

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A ::before / ::after pseudo-element only renders if it has a content property. Without content (even content: ""), the browser does not generate the box at all, so the color and weight have nothing to apply to.
commonMistakes: Assuming ::before inserts text from the HTML rather than from the content value.
Using a single colon and assuming it behaves differently (it does not for these legacy elements).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add the one declaration that makes the generated box exist and show a currency symbol.

files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 30px; font-size: 24px; }
.price::before { content: "$"; color: #16a34a; font-weight: 700; }

theory.question: What is the difference between a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element?
theory.directAnswer: A pseudo-class styles an element based on a state or structural condition it is in — like :hover, :focus, or :nth-child — using a single colon. A pseudo-element styles a specific sub-part or generated piece of an element — like ::before, ::after, or ::placeholder — using a double colon. Pseudo-classes select existing elements in a certain state; pseudo-elements create or target a fragment of an element.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Pseudo-classes are state/position filters on real elements; pseudo-elements are styleable sub-parts (some generated, some intrinsic like placeholder text).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To style interaction and decoration that the DOM doesn't expose directly, without adding markup or JavaScript.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser re-evaluates dynamic pseudo-classes on events and recomputes styles; for pseudo-elements it generates or targets an anonymous box (::before/::after need content).

theory.whyImportant: It is a foundational distinction asked in nearly every CSS interview, and the colon-count convention reflects it.
theory.realWorldExample: button:hover (pseudo-class) darkens a button while hovered; .label::after { content: ' *' } (pseudo-element) adds a required marker.

nestedTopics.title: Single vs double colon
nestedTopics.explanation: Pseudo-classes use :, pseudo-elements use ::; legacy pseudo-elements still accept a single colon.

nestedTopics.title: Generated content
nestedTopics.explanation: ::before/::after require a content property to render.

nestedTopics.title: State vs sub-part
nestedTopics.explanation: Pseudo-classes describe when an element matches; pseudo-elements describe which part of it you style.

followUps.question: Can you attach a click handler to ::before?
followUps.answer: No — generated content is render-only and not part of the DOM, so it cannot receive JavaScript events directly.

followUps.question: How many pseudo-elements can one selector have?
followUps.answer: Traditionally one per selector (e.g. one ::before), though newer specs allow some highlight pseudo-elements; ::before and ::after are separate so you can use both.

theory.question: Explain :nth-child versus :nth-of-type, and how the formula works.
theory.directAnswer: :nth-child(an+b) matches an element if it is at the matching position among ALL its siblings, regardless of type. :nth-of-type(an+b) counts only siblings of the same element type. The formula an+b is evaluated for n = 0, 1, 2…: 2n matches every even index, odd matches odd ones, and 3n+1 matches the 1st, 4th, 7th, and so on.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Structural pseudo-classes that select elements by sibling position.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To target patterns (every other row, the third item) without classes on each element.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: :nth-child checks position among all children; :nth-of-type filters to same-tag siblings first, then applies the index formula.

theory.whyImportant: Mixing them up is a classic bug — :nth-child(1) can fail to match if a different element precedes it.
theory.realWorldExample: tr:nth-child(even) stripes a table; p:nth-of-type(2) targets the second paragraph even if a heading comes first.

nestedTopics.title: The an+b formula
nestedTopics.explanation: n iterates 0,1,2…; 2n = even, 2n+1 = odd, -n+3 = first three.

nestedTopics.title: Keywords
nestedTopics.explanation: even and odd are shorthand for 2n and 2n+1.

followUps.question: How would you select the last three items?
followUps.answer: Use :nth-last-child(-n+3), which counts from the end.

scenario.question: Your buttons highlight on hover but keyboard users see no feedback when tabbing. How do you fix it accessibly?
scenario.directAnswer: Hover styles only fire for pointer users. Add a focus style so keyboard users get equivalent feedback — ideally :focus-visible to show a clear outline only during keyboard navigation, while keeping :hover for the mouse. Never remove the focus outline without replacing it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An accessibility gap from styling only the :hover state.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: :hover responds to pointer position; focus is a separate state triggered by tabbing or clicking.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Pair button:hover with button:focus-visible; :focus-visible uses browser heuristics to show the ring for keyboard but not mouse users.

scenario.whyImportant: Visible focus is a WCAG requirement; missing it makes keyboard navigation unusable.

nestedTopics.title: :focus vs :focus-visible
nestedTopics.explanation: :focus fires on any focus; :focus-visible shows the indicator mainly for keyboard interaction.

nestedTopics.title: outline best practice
nestedTopics.explanation: Restyle the outline rather than setting outline: none with no replacement.

followUps.question: Why prefer :focus-visible over :focus?
followUps.answer: It avoids showing a focus ring on mouse clicks while still showing it for keyboard users, giving a cleaner look without sacrificing accessibility.

coding.question: Write CSS to add even/odd zebra striping to a list and remove the bottom margin from the last item only.
coding.thoughtProcess: Zebra striping is a structural-pseudo-class job: :nth-child(even) and :nth-child(odd) target alternating items. For spacing, every item gets a bottom margin except the last, which is exactly what :not(:last-child) expresses, avoiding an overflow gap at the bottom.
coding.lineByLine: :nth-child(odd) shades the 1st, 3rd, 5th… items; :nth-child(even) shades the 2nd, 4th… items, producing stripes. :not(:last-child) applies the bottom margin to every item except the final one, so there is no trailing gap.

alternativeApproaches.title: gap on a flex/grid list
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Instead of margins, make .list a flex column with gap so spacing applies only between items automatically.

followUps.question: How would you stripe only every third row?

productionDeepDive.architecture: In design systems, pseudo-classes encode interactive states (hover/focus/active/disabled) as part of component recipes, and pseudo-elements provide decoration (icons, dividers, required markers, focus rings) without polluting markup. Centralizing state styles keeps components consistent and themeable.
productionDeepDive.performance: Selector matching for these is fast, but extremely broad dynamic selectors (universal :hover) and large generated-content trees can add style-recalc cost. Generated content avoids extra DOM nodes, which is usually cheaper than adding elements.
productionDeepDive.security: Generated content can echo attribute values via content: attr(...); never surface untrusted attributes you wouldn't trust as visible text, and remember pseudo-element content is not a substitute for accessible, secure markup.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Standardize focus and hover tokens (colors, outline widths) so every component shares the same interactive language; expose them as CSS variables to support theming at scale.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Always pair :hover with :focus-visible and document why decorative ::before/::after exist, since invisible generated boxes can confuse future maintainers debugging layout or accessibility.
productionDeepDive.observability: Browser DevTools lets you toggle element states (:hov panel) to inspect :hover/:focus/:active styles, and shows generated ::before/::after nodes in the elements tree — the fastest way to debug them.

caseStudies.problem: Needed consistent, accessible interactive states and decoration without extra markup.
caseStudies.solution: Encoded states with pseudo-classes and decoration with pseudo-elements, exposed via tokens.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Generated content is not reliably accessible, so essential info stays in real DOM.
caseStudies.lessons: Pseudo-selectors cover most interactive/decorative needs while keeping HTML clean.

projectBuilder.summary: Build a polished interactive card and form section using pseudo-classes for states and pseudo-elements for decoration.
requirements: A card with hover and keyboard-focus elevation states
A form with styled :placeholder, :required markers, and :checked custom checkbox
A list or table with zebra striping and tooltip via ::after
projectBuilder.architecture: Plain HTML with a single stylesheet: states via :hover/:focus-visible/:checked, decoration via ::before/::after, structure via :nth-child and :not().

steps.title: Card states
steps.instructions: Add :hover and :focus-visible styles that lift the card and show an outline.
steps.checkpoint: Card responds to both mouse hover and keyboard focus.

steps.title: Form decoration
steps.instructions: Style ::placeholder, add a red ::after asterisk to required labels, and build a :checked custom checkbox.
steps.checkpoint: Placeholders are muted, required fields are marked, and the checkbox toggles visually.

steps.title: List polish
steps.instructions: Add :nth-child striping, :not(:last-child) spacing, and a [data-tip]:hover::after tooltip.
steps.checkpoint: Rows are striped and a tooltip appears on hover.

interviewQuestions: Why does the custom checkbox use input:checked + label?
How do you keep the tooltip content accessible if ::after is not in the a11y tree?

keyTakeaways: Pseudo-classes (single colon) style elements by state or position; pseudo-elements (double colon) style or generate a sub-part of an element.
::before and ::after only render when a content property is set — even content: "".
:nth-child counts all siblings while :nth-of-type counts same-tag siblings; the an+b formula drives both.
Pair :hover with :focus-visible so keyboard users get equivalent, accessible feedback.
:checked + sibling selectors enable powerful CSS-only toggles, accordions, and custom form controls.
